topics.title: Rows, columns and records
topics.body: A row is one record and a column is one field across records. `len(df)` counts records, `df.columns` lists fields, and the two numbers answer different questions.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "city": ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune"]})
print(len(df), len(df.columns))
print(df["city"].nunique())

topics.title: Structured data has a schema
topics.body: A structured table has the same fields on every row with a type per field. Scraped text or a JSON blob is unstructured: it needs parsing before it can be counted.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

rows = [{"id": 1, "tags": "a"}, {"id": 2}]
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.notna().all(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: Pandas, Excel and SQL in one line
topics.body: Excel is a manual grid, SQL queries a database in place, Pandas runs code over data in memory. The same three operations — select, filter, group — exist in all of them.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
print(df[df["sales"] > 5].groupby("city")["sales"].sum().to_dict())

topics.title: pd is only an alias
topics.body: `import pandas as pd` binds the module to a short name; `pd` is a convention, not a requirement. Code that imports `pandas` keeps working but reads like everyone else's code does not.
topics.code:
import pandas as pandas_lib

df = pandas_lib.DataFrame({"a": [1]})
print(type(df).__name__)

interview.q: What is a DataFrame internally, in one sentence?
interview.answer: A dict-like collection of Series that share one index, with a column axis that carries names and dtypes. That is why selecting a column returns a Series and aligning two frames matches rows by label.

interview.q: When would a plain Python dict be enough instead of a DataFrame?
interview.answer: When the data is a single record, there are no repeated rows to aggregate, and no alignment or missing-value handling is needed. A one-row lookup is a dict; a table of many rows with grouping is a frame.

topics.title: Series from a dict keeps the keys
topics.body: A dict becomes a Series whose index is the keys in insertion order — the shortest way to carry named values with their labels.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series({"a": 10, "b": 20})
print(s.index.tolist())
print(s.sum())

topics.title: reindex asks for a different set of labels
topics.body: `reindex` lines the object up with the labels you name: existing ones keep their value, missing ones become NaN. It is the alignment tool.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20], index=["a", "b"])
print(s.reindex(["b", "c"]).tolist())

topics.title: set_index moves a column into the index
topics.body: `set_index` returns a new frame with that column as labels, which makes `.loc` lookups on it direct and keeps the column out of the data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [10, 20], "name": ["Aman", "Riya"]})
out = df.set_index("id")
print(out.index.tolist())
print(out.columns.tolist())

topics.title: A list of lists needs column names
topics.body: Row-wise input has no names, so `columns=` supplies them. Without it the columns are 0, 1, 2 and every later selection is positional.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [3, 4]], columns=["a", "b"])
print(df["b"].tolist())

interview.q: Why must an index be unique before a join?
interview.answer: A join matches labels, so a duplicate label on either side multiplies the matched rows into a fan-out. Convert to a key column and deduplicate before merging, or use `validate` so the duplicate fails loudly.

interview.q: What is the difference between `set_index` and `reset_index`?
interview.answer: `set_index` demotes a column into the row labels; `reset_index` promotes the labels back into a column and restores 0..n. They are inverses, and a round trip loses a meaningful index only if you choose to.

topics.title: sample shows rows you did not look at
topics.body: `head` and `tail` only show the edges. `sample(n, random_state=...)` draws from anywhere in the table, which is how a suspicious middle row is found.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": range(10)})
print(df.sample(2, random_state=1)["id"].tolist())

topics.title: select_dtypes picks by type
topics.body: `select_dtypes` returns only the columns of the types you name, so scaling, dates and text can be handled by separate pipelines.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [1.5], "c": ["x"]})
print(df.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist())

topics.title: empty answers a different question than zero rows
topics.body: `empty` is True when there are no elements at all — no rows OR no columns. A frame with rows and zero columns is empty too, which catches a wrong `usecols`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print(pd.DataFrame().empty)
print(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1]}).empty)

topics.title: count ignores missing, size does not
topics.body: `count` returns non-missing values per column; `size` returns rows × columns. Comparing them shows how much of a column is actually usable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3]})
print(df["a"].count(), df["a"].size)

interview.q: Why sample instead of only looking at head?
interview.answer: Sorted or grouped exports put the anomalies in the middle: a bad batch, a blank block, a wrong unit. A seeded sample reaches rows head and tail never show, and the seed keeps the review reproducible.

interview.q: What does a clean `describe()` still hide?
interview.answer: Shape. Identical mean, std and quartiles can describe a normal column and a bimodal one. Bin or plot the column before drawing a conclusion from the summary.

topics.title: at and iat read one cell fast
topics.body: `at` is a label lookup and `iat` is a positional one, both for a single scalar. They are the cheapest read when you know exactly which cell you need.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [10, 20]}, index=["x", "y"])
print(df.at["y", "a"], df.iat[0, 0])

topics.title: where keeps the shape, mask keeps the shape
topics.body: `where` keeps a value where the condition is True and replaces the rest; `mask` does the opposite. Both return the original shape, unlike filtering.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"v": [1, 5, 9]})
print(df.where(df["v"] > 4, 0)["v"].tolist())
print(df.mask(df["v"] > 4, 0)["v"].tolist())

topics.title: filter matches column names, not rows
topics.body: `filter(like=...)` selects columns by their name pattern. It is not a row filter; rows belong to a Boolean mask or `query`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sale_jan": [1], "sale_feb": [2], "cost": [3]})
print(df.filter(like="sale").columns.tolist())

topics.title: A mask combines with & only inside brackets
topics.body: `&` binds tighter than `>` in Python, so every comparison needs its own parentheses; `and` on an array raises because it wants one truth value.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 5, 9]})
print(df[(df["a"] > 2) & (df["a"] < 9)]["a"].tolist())

interview.q: When is `where` the right tool instead of a Boolean filter?
interview.answer: When the row count and index must stay intact — capping outliers, blanking invalid cells, or building two aligned branches. Filtering removes rows, so anything that must line up with the original frame needs `where` or `mask`.

interview.q: Why can a filter return an empty frame without any error?
interview.answer: Filtering is a comparison, and a comparison that matches nothing is perfectly valid. The cause is almost always dtype (text compared to a number), case or whitespace in a category, or a column name that silently differs.

topics.title: Nullable Int64 keeps integers and gaps
topics.body: The classic `int64` cannot hold NaN, so a gap forces float. The nullable `Int64` extension stores `pd.NA` and keeps the integer arithmetic.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, None], dtype="Int64")
print(s.dtype)
print(s.sum())

topics.title: A category dtype can be ordered
topics.body: Declaring the categories and `ordered=True` lets comparisons and sorting follow the domain order, which is what turns a status column into a sortable one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["medium", "low"], dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(["low", "medium", "high"], ordered=True))
print((s == "low").tolist())
print(s.cat.categories.tolist())

topics.title: to_datetime fixes the unit
topics.body: Passing `format=` or `unit=` makes parsing explicit. Without it pandas guesses, and two files in one pipeline can guess differently.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["05/01/2026"]), format="%d/%m/%Y")
print(s.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist())

topics.title: astype on one column only
topics.body: A per-column conversion keeps the rest of the frame untouched: build a dict or use `astype` on the Series, so a numeric column does not turn the whole frame into text.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["1", "2"], "name": ["a", "b"]})
df["id"] = df["id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).tolist())

interview.q: Why prefer an explicit dtype map over inference at load?
interview.answer: Inference changes with the data: one blank cell turns an integer column into float, and a join key that was numeric stops matching. An explicit map fails at the boundary, where the cause is obvious, instead of at the join.

interview.q: When is `object` dtype a real problem?
interview.answer: When the column holds numbers or repeated text: arithmetic either fails or falls back to Python, memory grows with pointer overhead, and grouping is slower. It is fine for genuinely heterogeneous values, which usually means the column should be split.
